hook.situation: A weekend plan keeps changing: you may go with a friend, you also need to email a teacher, you only have one hour, and you can do nothing but study. The nouns are simple; the particles decide the relationships.
objectives: Choose the right particle for receiver, companion, possession, also, only, scarcity, surprising amount, and minimum option.
Contrast similar particles such as 만 vs 밖에 and 도 vs 이라도.
Build real weekend-plan sentences instead of memorizing particle labels.
hook.whyItMatters: Korean particles are small, but they carry the grammar that English often puts in word order or prepositions. 친구, 친구에게, 친구랑, 친구도, 친구만, and 친구의 all start from the same noun but tell different stories.

grammarNotes.title: 에게 / 한테 / 께 — receiver or target person
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Use this set when an action points toward a person: giving, sending, asking, telling, or lending.
grammarNotes.formation: Attach directly to a person noun. 에게 is neutral/written, 한테 is conversational, and 께 is honorific for someone respected.

examples.en: I gave a gift to a friend.
examples.note: 친구 is the receiver, so 에게 fits.

examples.en: I lent a book to a friend.
examples.note: 한테 is the everyday spoken version.

examples.en: I sent an email to the teacher.
examples.note: 께 matches the respectful verb 드리다.

examples.en: I sent an email to the company.
examples.note: A company as an organization/place often takes 에, not 에게.

exceptions: For 'from a person', use 에게서 or 한테서: 친구에게서 들었어요.
Do not attach 에게 to objects: 선물에게 is wrong because 선물 is not the receiver person.

grammarNotes.title: 와/과 / 하고 / (이)랑 — and or with
grammarNotes.mentalModel: These connect nouns. The same particle can mean 'and' in a list or 'with' when the sentence describes doing something together.
grammarNotes.formation: 와 after a vowel-final noun, 과 after a consonant-final noun. 하고 attaches to any noun. 랑 follows a vowel-final noun, 이랑 follows a consonant-final noun.

examples.en: I watch a movie with a friend.
examples.note: 랑 is natural in casual speech.

examples.en: I prepared it together with Minsu.
examples.note: 하고 plus 같이 makes the 'with' meaning very clear.

examples.en: I bought coffee and water.
examples.note: 와/과 sounds more written or tidy.

examples.en: I brought only a book and a bag.
examples.note: 하고 links nouns before another particle appears.

exceptions: These particles connect nouns, not full clauses. For 'and then' between actions, use a connective like -고.
When you mean doing something together, 같이 often removes ambiguity.

grammarNotes.title: 밖에 + negative — nothing but / only because there is no more
grammarNotes.mentalModel: 밖에 is a limit with a negative ending. It feels like the options are restricted or insufficient.
grammarNotes.formation: Attach 밖에 to a noun, then use a negative idea such as 없어요, 안 해요, 못 해요, or -지 않아요.

examples.en: I can do nothing but study.
examples.note: 못 해요 supplies the required negative meaning.

examples.en: I only have one hour.
examples.note: 밖에 emphasizes that the time is limited.

examples.en: There is no way except this.
examples.note: A strong limited-choice frame.

examples.en: I can only drink water.
examples.note: 밖에 pairs with 못.

exceptions: Do not say 공부밖에 해요. 밖에 needs a negative predicate.
If you just mean neutral 'only', use 만: 공부만 해요.

grammarNotes.title: 이나 / 나 — as many as, surprisingly much
grammarNotes.mentalModel: 이나 after a number shows the amount feels bigger, longer, or more than expected.
grammarNotes.formation: Use 이나 after a consonant-final noun or number, 나 after a vowel-final noun or number.

examples.en: As many as three exam questions are left.
examples.note: The speaker feels three is a lot.

examples.en: I drank as many as five cups of coffee.
examples.note: 잔 ends in a consonant, so 잔이나.

examples.en: I waited for a whole hour.
examples.note: The time feels long to the speaker.

examples.en: As many as ten people came.
examples.note: 명 takes 이나 because it ends in a consonant.

exceptions: 이나 can have other meanings, such as 'or' in choices, but this chapter uses the surprising-amount meaning.
Do not confuse 이나 with 이라도. 커피를 다섯 잔이나 means the amount is surprisingly high; 커피라도 means coffee is a minimum option.

grammarNotes.title: 이라도 / 라도 — at least; even if only
grammarNotes.mentalModel: 라도 offers a minimum option when the ideal option is unavailable or uncertain.
grammarNotes.formation: Use 이라도 after a consonant-final noun and 라도 after a vowel-final noun.

examples.en: Do you want to at least drink coffee?
examples.note: Coffee is a small possible option, not the full plan.

examples.en: I want to meet even if only for a moment.
examples.note: 이라도 makes a small amount feel worthwhile.

examples.en: It would be good to prepare at least a small gift.
examples.note: 선물 ends in a consonant, so 선물이라도.

examples.en: Should I at least bring you water?
examples.note: A polite minimum offer.

exceptions: 라도 is not the same as 도. 선물도 means 'a gift too'; 선물이라도 means 'at least a gift.'
라도 often sounds like a fallback, compromise, or minimum acceptable option.

grammarNotes.title: 의 — possession and noun-to-noun link
grammarNotes.mentalModel: 의 links one noun to another: whose thing, what kind of thing, or what the second noun belongs to.
grammarNotes.formation: N의 N. In speech, 의 is often reduced or dropped, and pronouns contract: 저의 → 제, 나의 → 내.

examples.en: I need to return my friend's book.
examples.note: 친구의 책 marks whose book it is.

examples.en: I wrote my name too.
examples.note: 제 is the spoken contraction of 저의.

examples.en: Today's plan is studying.
examples.note: 의 can link a time noun to a plan or topic.

examples.en: It is my friend's bag.
examples.note: In speech, 의 is often dropped.

exceptions: Do not overuse 의 in every noun pair. 친구 집 and 한국어 수업 are natural without 의.
Pronouns are special: 저의 almost always becomes 제 in normal speech.

grammarNotes.title: 도 — also / too / even
grammarNotes.mentalModel: 도 adds something to an existing set. It can replace subject, object, or topic particles, and it can stack after place/time particles.
grammarNotes.formation: Attach 도 directly to the noun when it replaces 은/는/이/가/을/를. After place particles, use 에도 or 에서도.

examples.en: Are you also going to see a movie?
examples.note: 도 adds movie to another plan or activity.

examples.en: I also sent the teacher an email.
examples.note: 도 replaces 을/를 after 이메일.

examples.en: My friend does not have time either.
examples.note: 도 replaces 이/가 after 친구.

examples.en: I studied at the cafe too.
examples.note: 도 stacks after 에서.

exceptions: Do not keep 을/를 before 도: 이메일을도 is wrong; say 이메일도.
도 can mean 'even' in some contexts, but start with 'also/too' at this level.

grammarNotes.title: 만 — only / just
grammarNotes.mentalModel: 만 limits the focus neutrally. It does not require a negative ending.
grammarNotes.formation: Attach 만 directly to the noun or quantity. It replaces 은/는/이/가/을/를, but follows place/time particles such as 에서만.

examples.en: I want to rest for just one hour.
examples.note: 만 limits the amount of time.

examples.en: I only drank coffee.
examples.note: Positive predicate is fine with 만.

examples.en: I brought only the book.
examples.note: 만 replaces 을/를.

examples.en: I study only at home.
examples.note: After 에서, 만 stacks: 에서만.

exceptions: 만 is neutral; 밖에 feels limited and needs a negative: 커피만 마셨어요 vs 커피밖에 못 마셨어요.
Do not attach both object particle and 만: 책을만 is not the normal form; say 책만.

exampleSentence.en: Are you also going to see a movie with a friend this weekend?
I also sent the teacher an email.
I gave a gift to a friend.
I also need to send the teacher an email.
I also need to return my friend's book.
Are you also going to see a movie?
As many as three exam questions are left.
As many as three questions are left.
I can do nothing but study.
Do you want to at least drink coffee?
Should I at least bring you water?
There is no way except this.
I gave a gift to a friend.

extendedVocabulary.english: to give/send humbly to someone respected

exampleSentence.en: I sent the teacher an email.

extendedDialogue.setting: Two friends negotiate a weekend plan while one person has study obligations.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Are you also going to see a movie with a friend this weekend?
lines.grammarNote: 친구랑 marks companionship; 영화도 adds another activity.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 아니요, 시험 문제가 세 개나 남아서 공부밖에 못 해요.
lines.romanization: aniyo, siheom munjega se gaena namaseo gongbubakke mot haeyo.
lines.en: No, as many as three exam questions are left, so I can only study.
lines.grammarNote: 세 개나 shows the amount feels large; 밖에 pairs with 못 해요.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Then do you want to at least drink coffee? Just one hour.
lines.grammarNote: 라도 offers a minimum option; 만 limits the time.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 좋아요. 선생님께 이메일도 보내드리고, 친구의 책도 돌려줘야 해요.
lines.romanization: joayo. seonsaengnimkke imeildo bonaedeurigo, chinguui chaekdo dollyeojwoya haeyo.
lines.en: Sounds good. I also need to send the teacher an email and return my friend's book.
lines.grammarNote: 께 marks the respected receiver; 의 marks possession; 도 adds tasks.

readingText.title: 주말 계획을 입자로 정리하기
readingText.body: 주말 계획을 말할 때는 명사보다 입자가 더 많은 정보를 줄 때가 있어요. 친구랑 영화를 보면 함께 가는 사람을 말하는 것이고, 영화도 본다고 하면 다른 일에 영화를 추가하는 거예요. 시험 문제가 세 개나 남았다고 하면 양이 많게 느껴지고, 공부밖에 못 한다고 하면 선택지가 거의 없다는 뜻이에요. 그래도 커피라도 마시자고 하면 완전한 약속은 아니지만 최소한 가능한 제안을 하는 거예요. 마지막으로 선생님께 이메일을 보내드리고 친구의 책을 돌려줘야 한다면, 께는 받는 사람의 높임, 의는 소유 관계를 보여 줘요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: When talking about weekend plans, particles often carry more information than the noun itself. 친구랑 tells who you go with, 영화도 adds a movie to other plans, 세 개나 shows the amount feels large, 공부밖에 못 해요 means the options are limited, 커피라도 offers a minimum plan, 께 marks a respected receiver, and 의 marks possession.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 공부밖에 못 해요에서 왜 못 해요가 필요해요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 밖에가 부정 표현과 함께 쓰여서 선택지가 제한된다는 뜻을 만들기 때문이에요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 커피라도 마실래요?는 어떤 느낌이에요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 완전한 계획은 아니지만 최소한 커피라도 마시자는 제안이에요.

culturalNote.title: A small particle can change the social meaning
culturalNote.body: 선생님에게 이메일을 보냈어요 is grammatically possible, but 선생님께 이메일을 드렸어요 sounds more respectful because 께 and 드리다 work together. In everyday speech, Korean speakers also drop 의 often, but they keep particles like 께, 밖에, 만, and 도 when those particles carry important social or logical meaning.
culturalNote.tip: When a sentence feels wrong, do not only change the noun. Ask what relationship the particle is trying to mark: receiver, companion, possession, addition, limit, scarcity, large amount, or minimum option.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence correctly marks the teacher as a respected receiver?
inlineExercises.explanation: 께 marks a respected person receiving the action, and 드리다 matches the respectful tone.
밖에 needs a negative idea such as 못, 안, or 없어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'as many as three exam questions are left'?
inlineExercises.explanation: 이나/나 after a number shows the amount feels large or surprising.
라도 offers a minimum or fallback option.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which pair shows the difference between 만 and 밖에?
inlineExercises.explanation: 만 works with a positive predicate; 밖에 needs a negative predicate.
의 links 친구 to 책: the friend's book.

bullets: 에게/한테/께 marks a person receiving an action: 친구에게 선물을 줬어요, 선생님께 이메일을 드렸어요.
와/과/하고/(이)랑 links nouns or marks companionship: 친구랑 영화 봐요.
밖에 needs a negative predicate: 공부밖에 못 해요, 한 시간밖에 없어요.
이나/나 after a number shows a surprisingly large amount: 세 개나, 다섯 잔이나.
이라도/라도 offers a minimum option: 커피라도, 잠깐이라도.
의 marks possession or noun-to-noun relation, while 도 and 만 add or limit focus.
